why: The devices use UDP, and Global Accelerator supports UDP, routes users over the AWS backbone from the nearest edge location, and fails over between Regional endpoints in seconds. A Network Load Balancer handles UDP traffic, and ECS on Fargate processes the data without servers to manage.

others.A: Route 53 failover depends on DNS TTLs and health checks, so failover is slower, and an NLB cannot invoke a Lambda function directly.
others.C: An Application Load Balancer only handles HTTP and HTTPS, so it cannot receive UDP traffic.
others.D: An ALB cannot carry UDP, and Route 53 DNS failover is slower than Global Accelerator.

tip: UDP plus low latency plus fast Regional failover points to Global Accelerator with NLB endpoints.

why: A Compute Savings Plan covers EC2, Fargate and Lambda usage, so it keeps saving money as the number of Lambda functions grows, while an EC2 Instance Savings Plan covers only EC2. Connecting the Lambda functions to the private subnet that holds the EC2 instances gives them direct, low-latency network access.

others.A: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not apply to Lambda, so savings on the growing Lambda usage are lost.
others.B: An EC2 Instance Savings Plan does not cover Lambda, and a public subnet is not needed and does not give Lambda functions internet access or better latency.
others.D: Lambda functions in the Lambda service VPC cannot reach the EC2 instances in the private subnet directly.

tip: Savings that must cover Lambda or Fargate mean a Compute Savings Plan.

why: An SQS queue absorbs irregular, bursty batches of requests and decouples the API from processing. ECS services that read from the queue can scale both the cluster and the number of service tasks based on queue depth, including down to very little capacity when models are idle.

others.A: Models used for batch inference often exceed Lambda limits, and an NLB cannot invoke Lambda functions.
others.B: App Mesh is a service mesh for traffic routing; it does not scale ECS tasks based on queue size.
others.C: Lambda functions do not have configurable vCPUs that AWS Auto Scaling can increase; CPU is tied to memory settings.

tip: Irregular, bursty asynchronous work fits a queue with consumers that auto scale on queue depth.

why: Identity-based policies are attached to IAM identities: users, groups and roles. Of the choices, only Role and Group are IAM identities that can have this policy attached.

others.C: An AWS Organizations organization is controlled with service control policies, not identity-based IAM policies.
others.D: An ECS resource is not an IAM principal; ECS tasks receive permissions through an IAM role.
others.E: An EC2 resource is not an IAM principal; instances receive permissions through an instance profile role.

tip: Identity-based policies attach to users, groups and roles; resource-based policies attach to resources.

why: The Allow statement grants all EC2 actions, but only in us-east-1. The Deny statement blocks ec2:StopInstances and ec2:TerminateInstances whenever MFA is not present, so members can stop and terminate instances in us-east-1 only after signing in with MFA, and can perform any other EC2 action in us-east-1.

others.A: An explicit Deny is always evaluated and overrides the Allow, so the statement order does not cancel the Deny.
others.B: Only the stop and terminate actions are denied without MFA; other EC2 actions are allowed without MFA.
others.C: The Allow is limited to us-east-1 by the ec2:Region condition, so permissions do not apply to all Regions.

tip: An explicit Deny always wins, regardless of statement order; read each condition carefully.

why: AWS WAF attaches to an Application Load Balancer and supports rate-based rules that automatically block clients that send too many requests, even when the IP addresses keep changing. Legitimate users who stay under the limit are not affected.

others.A: Amazon Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities and cannot block incoming requests.
others.C: Network ACLs apply to subnets, need fixed IP ranges and cannot keep up with attackers that keep changing addresses.
others.D: GuardDuty detects threats but does not block traffic or offer rate limiting.

tip: Blocking floods of HTTP requests from changing IPs means AWS WAF rate-based rules.

why: A VPC can have secondary IPv4 CIDR blocks added at any time. Adding one and creating new subnets from it gives more IP addresses in the same VPC, with no peering, transit gateway or VPN to build and run.

others.B: A second VPC with peering adds routing and connection management, which is more overhead than extending the existing VPC.
others.C: A transit gateway and a second VPC add cost and routing work that the simple IP shortage does not need.
others.D: A self-managed VPN on EC2 between two VPCs is the most operational overhead of all the options.

tip: Running out of IPs in a VPC: add a secondary CIDR block.

why: The Management VPC connects to the data center through VPN tunnels that end on a single customer gateway device, which is a single point of failure. Adding a second set of VPN connections from a second customer gateway device removes it. The Production VPC already has two Direct Connect connections.

others.A: VPNs between the two VPCs do not address the single on-premises customer gateway.
others.B: A VPC can have only one virtual private gateway attached, and the gateway itself is already highly available.
others.D: VPC peering connections are already highly available, and only one peering connection can exist between two VPCs.

tip: For VPN resilience, look for a second customer gateway device on premises.

why: Amazon AppFlow is a fully managed integration service with a built-in Salesforce connector. It encrypts data in transit and can encrypt data at rest in S3 with a customer managed KMS key, so no custom code is needed.

others.A: Lambda functions would need custom code for the Salesforce API, authentication and encryption.
others.B: Step Functions orchestrates tasks but still needs custom code to move data from Salesforce.
others.D: Building a custom connector is unnecessary development work when AppFlow already supports Salesforce.

tip: SaaS (Salesforce, Zendesk, ServiceNow) to S3 transfers point to Amazon AppFlow.

why: The app uses both TCP and UDP, so it needs a Network Load Balancer, which supports both protocols. Global Accelerator also supports TCP and UDP and routes global users to the nearest edge location and over the AWS backbone, giving the lowest latency.

others.A: An Application Load Balancer only supports HTTP and HTTPS, so it cannot listen on UDP ports.
others.C: CloudFront only delivers HTTP and HTTPS traffic, so it cannot carry the app's UDP traffic.
others.D: CloudFront and an ALB both handle only HTTP and HTTPS, not UDP.

tip: TCP and UDP for global users means Global Accelerator in front of an NLB.

why: A gateway VPC endpoint for S3 is free and keeps traffic between the VPC and S3 on the AWS network. You associate it with route tables, so the containers reach S3 privately without NAT gateway data processing charges.

others.A: Intelligent-Tiering changes storage costs but does nothing to keep traffic off the internet.
others.B: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers over the internet through edge locations and costs extra.
others.D: Interface endpoints cost per hour and per GB, and they are not associated with route tables.

tip: Private, low-cost S3 access from a VPC means a gateway endpoint.

why: DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is an in-memory cache built for DynamoDB that gives microsecond read latency. It is API-compatible with DynamoDB, so the application only needs to switch to the DAX endpoint.

others.B: DynamoDB does not support read replicas; global tables replicate across Regions and do not lower read latency this way.
others.C: More read capacity reduces throttling but does not lower the latency of each read.
others.D: ElastiCache for Redis would need application code changes for caching logic, which goes against minimal changes.

tip: Faster DynamoDB reads with minimal code changes means DAX.

why: CloudFront caches static content at edge locations, so most requests never reach the ALB and EC2 instances. That reduces the load and the number of instances needed, and CloudFront data transfer is usually cheaper than serving from the origin.

others.B: An ALB cannot connect to ElastiCache to serve files, and ElastiCache is not meant for serving static web content.
others.C: AWS WAF filters requests; it cannot cache static files.
others.D: A second ALB in another Region adds infrastructure cost instead of reducing it.

tip: Static content plus rising traffic costs points to CloudFront caching.

why: The policy allows ec2:TerminateInstances, but an explicit Deny blocks the action when the request does not come from 192.0.2.0/24 or 203.0.113.0/24. The administrator's request came from another IP address, so the Deny applied and returned 403.

others.A: EC2 instances do not support resource-based policies.
others.B: Identity-based policies attached to a role do not include a Principal element; the principal is the role itself.
others.C: The Action field does grant ec2:TerminateInstances; the request fails because of the Deny condition.

tip: For an Access Denied puzzle, look for an explicit Deny with a condition such as NotIpAddress.

why: A transit gateway in the networking team's account can be shared with all other accounts through AWS RAM, and every VPC attaches to it in a hub-and-spoke design. This removes the need to manage a mesh of connections across hundreds of accounts.

others.A: A full mesh of VPC peering connections for hundreds of VPCs is very hard to manage.
others.B: Connecting VPCs over the internet through NAT and internet gateways is insecure and does not give private VPC-to-VPC routing.
others.D: A transit VPC with VPN gateways is a legacy design with far more operational work than Transit Gateway.

tip: Many VPCs across many accounts in one Region: share a Transit Gateway with AWS RAM.

why: DynamoDB global tables give a multi-Region, multi-active database where every Regional deployment can read and write locally and data replicates automatically. This meets the need for separate Regional deployments that share one reservation table.

others.B: Aurora cross-Region read replicas are read-only, so other Regions must still send writes to the primary Region.
others.C: RDS for MySQL read replicas in other Regions are also read-only and replicate asynchronously.
others.D: Separate Aurora Serverless databases kept in sync with custom Lambda code are complex and not globally consistent.

tip: Multi-Region reads and writes with low effort usually points to DynamoDB global tables. The community vote on this question is split with Aurora read replicas.

why: The two VPCs are in different Regions, so VPC peering works, but a security group rule cannot reference a security group in a peered VPC in another Region. The database security group must therefore allow the application servers' IP addresses, and the subnet route tables must be updated for the peering connection.

others.A: The inbound rule must be on the database security group in ap-southeast-2, not on the application security group in eu-west-1.
others.B: Security group references across an inter-Region peering connection are not supported.
others.D: Security group references are also not supported across inter-Region transit gateway peering.

tip: Security group references work across peered VPCs only in the same Region; across Regions, use CIDR or IP rules.

why: Cross-account IAM roles give temporary credentials through STS AssumeRole. Each business account trusts a specific role in the inventory account, so the application can read every team's table without any long-term secrets.

others.A: DynamoDB does not authenticate with secrets from Secrets Manager; access is controlled by IAM.
others.B: IAM users with long-term access keys that are rotated by hand are less secure than temporary role credentials.
others.D: DynamoDB does not support authentication with ACM certificates.

tip: Cross-account access, most securely: IAM roles with a trust policy and STS AssumeRole.

why: An RDS for MySQL Multi-AZ DB cluster gives standbys in multiple Availability Zones that can also serve reads. ElastiCache for Redis with replication is highly available for session data and read caching, and an Auto Scaling group across three AZs scales the web tier.

others.B: ElastiCache for Memcached has no replication, so cached session data is lost if a node fails.
others.C: Moving from MySQL to DynamoDB requires a rewrite of the application's data layer.
others.D: A single-AZ RDS instance is not highly available across Availability Zones.

tip: Session data that must survive failures belongs in Redis with replication, not Memcached.

why: Lambda, API Gateway and DynamoDB charge only for usage, which suits unpredictable traffic that can be idle for long periods. A Cognito user pool handles sign-up and sign-in for paying customers, and Amplify serves the static frontend through CloudFront.

others.B: ECS tasks, an ALB and RDS run all the time and cost money even when the site is idle.
others.D: Cognito identity pools grant AWS credentials; user pools are what authenticate users.
others.F: S3 static website hosting cannot run PHP, which is server-side code.

tip: User sign-in is a Cognito user pool; AWS credentials for users come from an identity pool.

why: A Route 53 failover (active-passive) routing policy sends traffic to the ALB while its health check passes and to a static error page in S3 when the check fails. It needs only DNS record changes and an S3 bucket, so changes and infrastructure are minimal.

others.A: Latency routing picks the fastest endpoint and could send users to the error page even when the site is healthy.
others.C: Running an EC2 instance for an error page adds infrastructure, and an active-active setup sends traffic to both endpoints.
others.D: Multivalue answer routing returns several healthy records at random and is not meant for primary and backup failover.

tip: Show a backup or error page when the primary fails: Route 53 failover routing to S3.

why: A NAT gateway in a public subnet lets instances in private subnets start outbound connections to the internet, such as calls to the third-party provider, while blocking inbound connections. It is a managed service, so there is no extra operational overhead.

others.A: A NAT instance is an EC2 instance that you must patch, scale and make highly available.
others.C: Routing private subnets to an internet gateway would make them public and does not work for instances without public IPs.
others.D: A virtual private gateway connects to on-premises networks through VPN, not to the internet.

tip: Outbound-only internet access for private subnets with low overhead: NAT gateway.

why: S3 Object Lambda runs a Lambda function on each GET request, so the PII can be redacted as files are read. The provider reads from the Object Lambda Access Point, no copies of the data are needed, and it scales automatically.

others.B: A custom web application on EC2 has to be built, scaled and maintained.
others.C: Copying non-PII data to DynamoDB changes the data format and adds a pipeline to maintain.

tip: Transform or redact S3 data as it is read: S3 Object Lambda.

why: S3 Storage Lens gives organization-wide visibility into all buckets across accounts and Regions, including data protection metrics that show which buckets do not have versioning enabled.

others.B: IAM Access Analyzer for S3 reports buckets that are shared or public, not their versioning status.
others.C: A Multi-Region Access Point routes requests across buckets in several Regions; it does not report bucket settings.

tip: Account-wide or organization-wide S3 usage and configuration metrics point to S3 Storage Lens.
